proposal: Lassman recommends repealing the Jones Act, the 1920 law requiring ships that carry cargo between U.S. ports to be U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed, arguing it has shrunk the U.S. fleet and raised shipping costs. The next administration should unilaterally grant Jones Act exemptions wherever the law allows, as is often done in hurricane season, and work with Congress to repeal the law.

status_summary: The first half of the recommendation, exemptions where allowed, is partly met by a temporary waiver; the repeal half has not advanced. The White House announced a Jones Act waiver in March 2026 that lets foreign-flag vessels carry oil, fuel and fertilizer between U.S. ports, with the administration saying it would reduce short-term disruption in the oil market (Cato, 2026-03-18; Argus describes the issue date as 17 March and links it to a U.S.-Iran war). The waiver was extended by 90 days on 2026-04-24 (NEFI) and again, by DHS, from 2026-08-17 through 2026-11-15, with the covered product list cut from more than 600 tariff codes in April to 237 and a vessel availability request required before voyages (AJOT, 2026-08-18). MARAD's domestic shipping page confirms waiver dates of 2026-03-17, 2026-05-18 and 2026-08-17 and waiver-voyage reports through October 2026. On repeal, Sen. Lee and Rep. McClintock introduced the Open America's Waters Act (S. 2043 and H.R. 3940) on 2025-06-12; no committee action or administration proposal was found, and the law remains in force. NEFI and 14 other trade associations wrote to congressional leaders on 2026-04-23 urging permanent reform, and 52 House Republicans, including the Speaker, signed a 2026-06-30 letter urging that the waiver not be renewed (Argus). No waiver document appears in a Federal Register search for the Jones Act since 2025-01-20.

timeline.event: Sen. Lee (S. 2043) and Rep. McClintock (H.R. 3940) introduce the Open America's Waters Act, 'to repeal the Jones Act restrictions on coastwise trade': it rewrites 46 U.S.C. 12112(a) so any vessel that qualifies under U.S. law may receive a coastwise endorsement, directs the Coast Guard to issue implementing regulations within 90 days, and repeals the section on loss of coastwise privileges. The bills were referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; no committee action or administration endorsement was found.

MARAD's domestic shipping page lists a Jones Act waiver dated 2026-03-17, an extension dated 2026-05-18 and a further extension dated 2026-08-17, and posts monthly waiver-voyage reports under 46 U.S.C. 501(c) from April through October 2026; the page does not state the waiver's scope, cargo types or expiration dates and does not link the waiver documents themselves.

Cato Institute reports that the White House has announced a 60-day suspension of the Jones Act for energy products and fertilizer moved within the United States, to mitigate short-term disruption in the oil market.
NEFI and 14 national trade associations send congressional leaders a letter calling for permanent Jones Act reform.
The White House announces a 90-day extension of the waiver, moving expiry from May 17 to mid-August, citing new data that more supply reached U.S. ports faster.
52 House Republicans, including the Speaker, sign a letter urging the President not to renew the waiver (reported 2026-07-01); no repeal bill is mentioned.

CBP guidance (CSMS 69519766) says DHS approved, at the request of the Department of War, a second 90-day extension of the 2026-03-17 waiver, effective 2026-08-17 and covering products loaded before 23:59 ET on 2026-11-15, with a vessel availability request explaining the national defense purpose and a post-voyage report to MARAD required.

The waiver is extended 90 days, through 2026-11-15; the covered product list falls to 237 tariff codes and foreign-vessel use requires a vessel availability request to DoW, MARAD and CBP (abbreviations as given in the source).

MARAD posts 12 waiver-voyage reports dated 2026-09-08 through 2026-09-29 under the 2026-08-17 extension, showing the waiver in use in September 2026 (the index page does not state cargo types, vessel flags or the expiry).
